claim: Data from plasma samples of 318 Tanzanian and 416 Dutch individuals were included in this study.
source: Data from plasma samples of 318 Tanzanian and 416 Dutch individuals were included in this study.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the sample sizes used in the study, which is verifiable from the study design.

claim: The Tanzanians had a significantly higher median age (30.2 years; 23.4–39.9) than the Dutch (23.0 years; 21.0–26.0; p-value <0.0001).
source: The Tanzanians had a significantly higher median (IQR) age (30.2 years; 23.4–39.9) than the Dutch (23.0 years; 21.0–26.0; p-value <0.0001) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of age data between the two cohorts, with p-value provided.

claim: Tanzanian females had a higher BMI than Dutch females (25.7; 22.6–29.9 vs. 21.5; 20.4–23.1; p-value <0.0001).
source: Tanzanian females also had a higher BMI than Dutch females (25.7; 22.6–29.9 vs. 21.5; 20.4–23.1; p-value <0.0001) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of BMI data between female participants in the two cohorts.

claim: The inflammatory proteome was measured using the Olink 'inflammation' panel, which targets 92 cytokines, chemokines and other inflammation and metabolism-related proteins.
source: Plasma proteins were measured with the Olink 92 Inflammation panel using proximity extension technology (Olink Proteomics AB, Uppsala, Sweden) (Assarsson et al., 2014). This panel includes 92 inflammation-related proteins.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the measurement platform used, with citation to the technology.

claim: Eighteen proteins were excluded from further analysis because their value was below the lower limit of detection in more than 25% of samples in both cohorts.
source: Eighteen proteins were excluded from further analysis because their value was below the lower limit of detection in more than 25% of samples in both cohorts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on data quality criteria.

claim: Principal component analysis of the remaining 74 proteins revealed a clear separation between Tanzanian and Dutch samples.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of the remaining 74 proteins revealed a clear separation between Tanzanian and Dutch samples (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 35 (47%) proteins were significantly higher in the Tanzanians and 20 (27%) lower at an FDR p<0.05, with correction for age and sex and BMI.
source: A volcano plot of differentially expressed proteins (Figure 1B) showed that 35 (47%) proteins were significantly higher in the Tanzanians and 20 (27%) lower at an FDR p<0.05, with correction for age and sex and BMI.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis with statistical correction for confounders.

claim: The most prominently upregulated protein in Tanzanians was 4E-BP1 (log2 FC 1.9; FDR p=1.3 × 10–60).
source: The most prominently (fold change (FC)) upregulated proteins were two regulators of metabolism: the mTOR substrate and translational repressor 4E-BP1 (log2 FC 1.9; FDR p=1.3 × 10–60)
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis with fold change and statistical significance values.

claim: FGF21 was prominently upregulated in Tanzanians (log2 FC 1.3; p=1.3 × 10–30).
source: and FGF21 (fibroblast growth factor 21; log2 FC 1.3; p=1.3 × 10–30), a hormone produced by the liver that functions as a major regulator of glucose and lipid homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis with fold change and statistical significance values.

claim: FGF21 is a hormone produced by the liver that functions as a major regulator of glucose and lipid homeostasis.
source: and FGF21 (fibroblast growth factor 21; log2 FC 1.3; p=1.3 × 10–30), a hormone produced by the liver that functions as a major regulator of glucose and lipid homeostasis.
evidence: This is established biological knowledge about FGF21 function.

claim: Obesity and excess carbohydrate and/or insufficient protein intake were reported to increase FGF21 concentrations.
source: Obesity and excess carbohydrate and/or insufficient protein intake were reported to increase FGF21 concentrations (Hill et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: IL-17A was upregulated in Tanzanians (log2 FC 0.7; p=9.6 × 10–34).
source: Other prominently upregulated proteins in the Tanzanians were interleukin (IL)–17 A (log2 FC 0.7; p=9.6 × 10–34)
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis with fold change and statistical significance values.

claim: IL-17C was upregulated in Tanzanians (log2 FC 0.7; p=1.1 × 10–74).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis with fold change and statistical significance values.

claim: CCL11/eotaxin was upregulated in Tanzanians (log2 FC 0.7; p=7.3 × 10–63).
source: and the CC-chemokine family members CCL11/eotaxin (eosinophil chemoattractant; log2 FC 0.7; p=7.3 × 10–63)
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis with fold change and statistical significance values.

claim: CCL3/MIP-1α was upregulated in Tanzanians (log2 FC 0.6; p=5.6 × 10–10).
source: CCL3/MIP-1α (macrophage inflammatory protein-1α; log2 FC 0.6; p=5.6 × 10–10)
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis with fold change and statistical significance values.

claim: CCL7/MCP3 was upregulated in Tanzanians (log2 FC 0.6; p=7.4 × 10–42).
source: CCL7/MCP3 (monocyte chemotactic protein 3; log2 FC 0.6; p=7.4 × 10–42)
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis with fold change and statistical significance values.

claim: CCL8/MCP2 was upregulated in Tanzanians (log2 FC 0.5; p=8.4 × 10–23).
source: and CCL8/MCP2 (log2 FC 0.5; p=8.4 × 10–23).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis with fold change and statistical significance values.

claim: TNF, IL-6, IL-10, and IL-18, as well as oncostatin-M (OSM) and adenosine deaminase (ADA) were significantly higher in the Tanzanians.
source: The cytokines Tumour Necrosis Factor (TNF), IL-6, IL-10, and IL-18, as well as oncostatin-M (OSM) and adenosine deaminase (ADA) were also significantly higher in the Tanzanians.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis results.

claim: ST1A1 was the most prominently downregulated protein in Tanzanians (log2 FC –0.8; p=2.2 × 10–16).
source: The most prominently downregulated proteins in Tanzanians were ST1A1 (sulfotransferase 1A1; log2 FC –0.8; p=2.2 × 10–16)
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis with fold change and statistical significance values.

claim: AXIN1 was prominently downregulated in Tanzanians (log2 FC –0.7; p=6.5 × 10–18).
source: and AXIN1 (axis inhibition protein 1; log2 FC –0.7; p=6.5 × 10–18).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis with fold change and statistical significance values.

claim: ST1A1 is a cytosolic sulfotransferase that catalyzes the sulfonation of endogenous and exogenous compounds.
source: ST1A1 is a cytosolic sulfotransferase that catalyzes the sulfonation of endogenous and exogenous compounds (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established biological knowledge about ST1A1 function, supported by citation.

claim: AXIN1 is a negative regulator of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway.
source: AXIN1 is a negative regulator of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway (Kikuchi, 1999).
evidence: This is established biological knowledge about AXIN1 function, supported by citation.

claim: The Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway is increasingly recognized to play an important role in inflammatory diseases, diabetes and cancer.
source: This pathway is increasingly recognized to play an important role in inflammatory diseases, diabetes and cancer (Jridi et al., 2020; Das et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CDCP1 was significantly up-regulated in the Tanzanian cohort (log2 FC 0.7; p=1.8 × 10–61).
source: Conversely, CDCP1 (CUB domain-containing protein 1), a transmembrane receptor that is a Wnt signaling promoter (He et al., 2020) was significantly up-regulated (log2 FC 0.7; p=1.8 × 10–61) in the Tanzanian cohort
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis with fold change and statistical significance values.

claim: CDCP1 is a transmembrane receptor that is a Wnt signaling promoter.
source: Conversely, CDCP1 (CUB domain-containing protein 1), a transmembrane receptor that is a Wnt signaling promoter (He et al., 2020)
evidence: This is established biological knowledge about CDCP1 function, supported by citation.

claim: The upregulation of CDCP1 and downregulation of AXIN1 suggest enhanced activity of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway in the Tanzanian participants.
source: suggesting enhanced activity of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway in the Tanzanian participants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential expression of CDCP1 and AXIN1 and their known roles in the Wnt pathway.

claim: Tanzanians had lower levels of the CXC chemokine family members CXCL1, CXCL5, CXCL6, and CXCL8 (IL8).
source: Finally, Tanzanians had lower levels of the CXC chemokine family members CXCL1, CXCL5, CXCL6, and CXCL8 (IL8).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis results.

claim: CXC chemokines mediate among others neutrophil trafficking.
source: These chemokines mediate among others neutrophil trafficking (Palomino and Marti, 2015).
evidence: This is established biological knowledge about CXC chemokine function, supported by citation.

claim: Tanzanian participants have significantly higher plasma concentrations of IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra), IL-6, and IL-18 than Dutch participants after correcting for age, sex, and BMI.
source: The data have been reported previously (Temba et al., 2022), and confirm that Tanzanian participants have significantly higher plasma concentrations of IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra), IL-6, and IL-18, together with significantly higher leptin and lower adiponectin concentrations than Dutch participants after correcting for age, sex, and BMI (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously reported data with statistical correction for confounders.

claim: Tanzanian participants have significantly higher leptin and lower adiponectin concentrations than Dutch participants after correcting for age, sex, and BMI.
source: The data have been reported previously (Temba et al., 2022), and confirm that Tanzanian participants have significantly higher plasma concentrations of IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra), IL-6, and IL-18, together with significantly higher leptin and lower adiponectin concentrations than Dutch participants after correcting for age, sex, and BMI (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by previously reported data with statistical correction for confounders.

claim: Tanzanian females regardless of BMI had higher plasma concentrations of leptin compared to Dutch females.
source: In addition, Tanzanian females regardless of BMI had higher plasma concentrations of leptin compared to Dutch females (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) in line with the previous findings (Abbas et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: There were no significant differences in plasma concentrations of resistin and alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) between Tanzanians and Dutch.
source: There were no significant differences in plasma concentrations of resistin and alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of these specific proteins.

claim: In the Dutch participants, advancing age was associated with an increase in inflammation-related proteins, including inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-7, IL-18), IL-15RA, monocyte chemoattractant proteins (MCP2-4), matrix metalloprotease1 (MMP1), the chemokine IL-8 and hepatocyte growth factor (HGF).
source: In the Dutch participants, advancing age was indeed associated with an increase in inflammation-related proteins, including inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-7, IL-18), IL-15RA, monocyte chemoattractant proteins (MCP2-4), matrix metalloprotease1 (MMP1), the chemokine IL-8 and hepatocyte growth factor (HGF).
evidence: This claim is supported by association analysis between age and protein levels in the Dutch cohort.

claim: The significant associations between advancing age and inflammatory proteins observed in the Dutch were largely absent in the Tanzanians.
source: In contrast, these significant associations were largely absent in the Tanzanians (Figure 2A, B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative association analysis between the two cohorts.

claim: Advancing age was strongly positively associated with CDCP1, CCL11, and CCL25 in both Tanzanian and Dutch cohorts.
source: An exception was a strong significant positive association of advancing age with CDCP1, CCL11, and CCL25, which was also observed in the Dutch cohort.
evidence: This claim is supported by association analysis in both cohorts.

claim: The association between advancing age and inflammatory markers is much weaker in Tanzanians than in Dutch.
source: Overall, these results show that the association between advancing age and inflammatory markers is much weaker in Tanzanians.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the comparative association analyses.

claim: Females in both cohorts overall had lower concentrations of inflammatory proteins than males.
source: Females in both cohorts overall had lower concentrations of inflammatory proteins than males (Figure 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by sex-stratified analysis of protein levels.

claim: Tanzanian females had significantly higher concentrations of TNF-beta (TNFB), IL12-beta and CCL28 than Tanzanian males.
source: Results also showed that Tanzanian females had significantly higher concentrations of TNF-beta (TNFB), IL12-beta and CCL28 than Tanzanian males.
evidence: This claim is supported by sex-stratified analysis within the Tanzanian cohort.

claim: There was no significant association between inflammatory proteins and environmental exposures such as type of toilet, exposure to wood smoke for cooking, farm-animal exposure, access to clean water, previous infections and prior use of antibiotics in Tanzanians.
source: Our results did not show a significant association between inflammatory proteins with one of these exposures.
evidence: This claim is supported by association analysis between environmental factors and protein levels.

claim: Unsupervised hierarchical clustering of food-derived metabolites yielded two different clusters (food-metabolome clusters one and two).
source: Using these metabolites, we first performed unsupervised hierarchical clustering, which yielded two different clusters (food-metabolome clusters one and two) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering analysis of metabolite data.

claim: Participants in food-metabolome cluster one more frequently consumed ugali (a traditional porridge made from maize), plantain (cooking banana) and green vegetables, and less frequently rice and fried potato chips.
source: Weekly food consumption was associated with these food-metabolome clusters: participants in cluster one more frequently consumed ugali (a traditional porridge made from maize), plantain (cooking banana) and green vegetables, and less frequently rice and fried potato chips (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by association analysis between food consumption patterns and metabolite clusters.

claim: Unsupervised clustering of the inflammatory proteome revealed two significant inflammatory proteome clusters: one with lower and one with higher expressed inflammatory proteins.
source: Next, we performed unsupervised clustering of the inflammatory proteome with age, sex, BMI, geolocation (i.e. rural vs. urban living), seasonality and the food-metabolome clusters as input variables. This analysis revealed two significant inflammatory proteome clusters: one with lower and one with higher expressed inflammatory proteins (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering analysis of proteomic data.

claim: Participants belonging to food-metabolome cluster one (i.e. more 'traditional' Tanzanian diet) were overrepresented in the cluster with lower-expressed inflammatory proteins.
source: Participants belonging to food-metabolome cluster one (i.e. more 'traditional' Tanzanian diet) were overrepresented in the cluster with lower-expressed inflammatory proteins, whereas participants belonging to cluster two were overrepresented in the cluster of higher-expressed inflammatory proteins (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by association analysis between metabolite clusters and protein expression clusters.

claim: Participants belonging to food-metabolome cluster two were overrepresented in the cluster of higher-expressed inflammatory proteins.
source: Participants belonging to food-metabolome cluster one (i.e. more 'traditional' Tanzanian diet) were overrepresented in the cluster with lower-expressed inflammatory proteins, whereas participants belonging to cluster two were overrepresented in the cluster of higher-expressed inflammatory proteins (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by association analysis between metabolite clusters and protein expression clusters.

claim: Age, sex and season were not associated with the inflammatory clustering in Tanzanians.
source: Other factors such as age, sex or season were not associated with the inflammatory clustering.
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering analysis that included these variables.

claim: There are negative associations between plant-derived polyphenols (apigenin, naringenin, cyanidin 3-(6-caffeoyl glucoside) 5-glucoside, licoagrodin, shoyuflavone C and phenolic acids such as gallic acid) and inflammatory proteins, particularly the MCP and CXCL families.
source: Results show different negative associations between plant-derived polyphenols (apigenin, naringenin, cyanidin 3-(6-caffeoyl glucoside) 5-glucoside, licoagrodin, shoyuflavone C and phenolic acids such as gallic acid) and inflammatory proteins, particularly the MCP and CXCL families (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between metabolites and proteins.

claim: There are positive associations between inflammatory proteins, especially members of the MCP and CXCL families, with plasma metabolites belonging to carboxylic acids and derivatives, organooxygen compounds, and prenol lipids.
source: In contrast, positive associations were observed between inflammatory proteins, and especially members of the MCP and CXCL families, with plasma metabolites belonging to the following classes: carboxylic acids and derivatives (e.g. aminobutanoic acid-ABA), organooxygen compounds (for example, triose), and prenol lipids such as resveratrol 4"-(6-) galloylglucoside (Figure 4, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between metabolites and proteins.

claim: A traditional plant-based Tanzanian diet in healthy Tanzanians has an important impact on circulating inflammatory proteins.
source: Overall, these findings support the notion that a traditional plant-based Tanzanian diet in healthy Tanzanians has an important impact on circulating inflammatory proteins.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the associations between diet-related metabolites and inflammatory proteins.

claim: A 2-week dietary switch from a westernized to a traditional Tanzanian, high-fiber, plant-based diet resulted in a significant reduction in plasma levels of 4E-BP1 (beta coeff. –1.87; p=0.003).
source: Using the same Olink proteomics platform, we observed a significant reduction in plasma levels of proteins associated with the mTOR pathway, including 4E-BP1 (beta coeff. –1.87; p=0.003)
evidence: This claim is supported by data from a dietary intervention study.

claim: A 2-week dietary switch from a westernized to a traditional Tanzanian, high-fiber, plant-based diet resulted in a significant reduction in plasma levels of FGF-19 (beta coeff. –1.253; p=0.0001).
source: and FGF-19 (beta coeff. –1.253; p=0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from a dietary intervention study.

claim: A 2-week dietary switch from a westernized to a traditional Tanzanian, high-fiber, plant-based diet showed a trend towards a reduction in AXIN1 (beta coeff. –0.555; p=0.063).
source: Additionally, we noticed a trend towards a reduction in the Wnt/ β -catenin signaling protein AXIN1 (beta coeff. –0.555; p=0.063)
evidence: This claim is supported by data from a dietary intervention study, though the result did not reach statistical significance.

claim: A 2-week dietary switch from a westernized to a traditional Tanzanian, high-fiber, plant-based diet did not change CDCP1 levels (beta coeff. 0.049; p=0.464).
source: while CDCP1 levels remained unchanged (beta coeff. 0.049; p=0.464).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from a dietary intervention study showing no significant change.

claim: Healthy Tanzanians have a more prominent pro-inflammatory phenotype compared to healthy Dutch individuals.
source: Our analysis of the inflammatory proteome shows that healthy Tanzanians have a more prominent pro-inflammatory phenotype compared to healthy Dutch individuals.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the differential expression analysis of inflammatory proteins.

claim: Among the Tanzanians, food-derived metabolites were identified as an important driver of variation in inflammation-related proteins.
source: Among the Tanzanians, food-derived metabolites were identified as an important driver of variation in inflammation-related proteins, emphasizing the potential importance of lifestyle changes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the association analyses between metabolites and proteins.

claim: There are remarkable differences in the genetic regulation of immune responses between Tanzanian and Dutch cohorts, with ancestry-specific pathways regulating induced cytokine responses and significant enrichment of the interferon pathway in the Tanzanians.
source: In the same European and African cohorts, we recently showed remarkable differences in the genetic regulation of immune responses, with ancestry-specific pathways regulating induced cytokine responses and significant enrichment of the interferon pathway in the Tanzanians (Boahen et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work in the same cohorts.

claim: The natural selection of genotypes that mediate a strong inflammatory response offers an obvious advantage in areas with a high infectious diseases burden such as sub-Saharan Africa.
source: From a historical perspective, the natural selection of genotypes that mediate a strong inflammatory response offers an obvious advantage in areas with a high infectious diseases burden such as sub-Saharan Africa.
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary principles and the historical disease burden in sub-Saharan Africa.

claim: A strong inflammatory response can be advantageous in the host's response against infections.
source: However, while a strong inflammatory response can be advantageous in the host's response against infections, it may become disadvantageous when the environment changes with a reduction in the infectious burden and a shift toward an unhealthy lifestyle.
evidence: This is based on established immunological knowledge about the role of inflammation in infection control.

claim: A strong inflammatory response may become disadvantageous when the environment changes with a reduction in the infectious burden and a shift toward an unhealthy lifestyle.
source: However, while a strong inflammatory response can be advantageous in the host's response against infections, it may become disadvantageous when the environment changes with a reduction in the infectious burden and a shift toward an unhealthy lifestyle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the epidemiological transition and the role of inflammation in NCDs.

claim: Many areas in sub-Saharan Africa are currently witnessing changes with a reduction in the infectious burden and a shift toward an unhealthy lifestyle, which is one of the important drivers of the rapid increase in non-communicable diseases.
source: Many areas in sub-Saharan Africa are currently witnessing such changes and this is one of the important drivers of the rapid increase in non-communicable diseases and other inflammation-associated pathologies.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the epidemiological transition in sub-Saharan Africa.

claim: Tanzanians who consumed more traditional staple foods, such as ugali or plantain, as well as green vegetables, had lower concentrations of inflammation-related proteins.
source: In the present study, we show that Tanzanians who consumed more traditional staple foods, such as ugali (porridge made from maize or millet) or plantain, as well as green vegetables, had lower concentrations of inflammation-related proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by association analysis between dietary patterns and protein levels.

claim: Gallic acid, a natural phenic acid present in mangos and other edible plants, had different negative associations with immune-derived proteins.
source: Especially gallic acid, a natural phenic acid with different health benefits, which is present in mangos and other edible plants (Kim et al., 2021), had different negative associations with immune-derived proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis and citation to literature about gallic acid.

claim: Diet has an important impact on cytokine responses in Tanzanians.
source: These data confirm our earlier findings that diet has an important impact on cytokine responses (Temba et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work in the same cohort.

claim: Diet has an important impact on plasmatic coagulation in Tanzanians.
source: as well as plasmatic coagulation (Temba et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work in the same cohort.

claim: Traditional foods, particularly plant-based diets, are increasingly recognized for their cardiovascular health benefits.
source: Traditional foods, particularly plant-based diets, are increasingly recognized for their cardiovascular health benefits (Hemler and Hu, 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Promoting traditional diets may be a viable public health strategy for curbing the NCDs epidemic.
source: and our findings support the notion that promoting traditional diets may be a viable public health strategy for curbing the NCDs epidemic.
evidence: This is an inference based on the associations between traditional diet and lower inflammatory protein levels.

claim: There were no significant associations between inflammatory proteins and environmental exposures such as pit latrine use, smoky fuels, or infections in Tanzanians.
source: Other environmental exposures may potentially confound the diet-inflammation associations, for example, individuals with a traditional diet may also use more frequently a pit latrine or smoky fuels and may have more infections, but we found no significant associations between inflammatory proteins and any of these other environmental exposures.
evidence: This claim is supported by association analysis between environmental factors and protein levels.

claim: In historically wealthy countries, aging is associated with a blunted response of immune cells to stimulation, while having a chronic low-inflammation state.
source: In historically wealthy countries, aging is associated with a blunted response of immune cells to stimulation, while having a chronic low-inflammation state (Yashin and Jazwinski, 2014; Liberale et al., 2020), as also observed in Dutch in this study.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and confirmed by data in the Dutch cohort.

claim: Cytokine responses decline in the Tanzanians with advancing age.
source: Cytokine responses decline in the Tanzanians with advancing age (Temba et al., 2021), similar to Europeans
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work in the same cohort.

claim: The reasons why systemic inflammation does not increase with age in Tanzanians remain uncertain.
source: but the reasons why systemic inflammation does not increase remain uncertain.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of uncertainty about the mechanisms underlying the observed pattern.

claim: Possible explanations for the lack of age-associated increase in systemic inflammation in Tanzanians include the already present inflammatory signature at a younger age, possibly because of higher cumulative exposure to infections or other environmental insults, or that older participants in Tanzania manage to control the inflammatory state by a healthier lifestyle.
source: Possible explanations are the already present inflammatory signature at a younger age, possibly because of higher cumulative exposure to infections or other environmental insults, or that older participants in Tanzania manage to control the inflammatory state by a healthier lifestyle.
evidence: These are speculative explanations for the observed pattern.

claim: FGF21 has received much attention recently as an endocrine regulator of glucose, lipid, and energy metabolism.
source: FGF21 has received much attention recently as an endocrine regulator of glucose, lipid, and energy metabolism (Hill et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: FGF21 is an insulin sensitizer.
source: FGF21 is an insulin sensitizer, and its secretion is increased by a high intake of carbohydrates and low dietary protein intake (Maekawa et al., 2017; Lundsgaard et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FGF21 secretion is increased by a high intake of carbohydrates and low dietary protein intake.
source: FGF21 is an insulin sensitizer, and its secretion is increased by a high intake of carbohydrates and low dietary protein intake (Maekawa et al., 2017; Lundsgaard et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FGF21 inhibits age-associated metabolic syndrome and protects against diabetic cardiomyopathy.
source: FGF21 inhibits age-associated metabolic syndrome and protects against diabetic cardiomyopathy (Yan et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: FGF21 acts differently from classic energy balance signals like leptin.
source: FGF21, therefore, acts differently from classic energy balance signals like leptin (Hill et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Traditional Tanzanian diets are high in carbohydrates and low in proteins.
source: Traditional Tanzanian diets are high in carbohydrates and low in proteins, which may explain the high FGF21 among the Tanzanians.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of traditional Tanzanian dietary patterns and is used to infer the reason for high FGF21.

claim: The high FGF21 among Tanzanians may be explained by their traditional diets being high in carbohydrates and low in proteins.
source: Traditional Tanzanian diets are high in carbohydrates and low in proteins, which may explain the high FGF21 among the Tanzanians.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known dietary patterns and the known regulation of FGF21.

claim: FGF21 was reported to be higher in obesity.
source: FGF21 was also reported to be higher in obesity (Zhang et al., 2008), but we did not find an association with BMI.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature, but the authors note they did not observe this association in their data.

claim: There was no association between FGF21 and BMI in this study.
source: FGF21 was also reported to be higher in obesity (Zhang et al., 2008), but we did not find an association with BMI.
evidence: This claim is supported by the absence of a significant association in the data analysis.

claim: An earlier study among non-obese and obese subjects with type 2 diabetes in Tanzania and Sweden showed that leptin concentrations were 50% higher in the Tanzanians.
source: This is in line with the results of an earlier study among non-obese and obese subjects with type 2 diabetes in Tanzania and Sweden, which showed that leptin concentrations were 50% higher in the Tanzanians (Abbas et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The findings support the importance of potential ethnic differences in metabolic profiles and adipocytokines.
source: This supports the importance of potential ethnic differences in metabolic profiles and adipocytokines (Mente et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences and is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: This study is the first to compare FGF21 levels between healthy individuals from sub-Saharan Africa and Europe.
source: To our knowledge, this study is the first to compare FGF21 levels between healthy individuals from sub-Saharan Africa and Europe.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: The Wnt/β-catenin pathway is a key regulator of inflammation, playing a role in both the inflammatory and anti-inflammatory pathways.
source: The Wnt/β-catenin pathway is a key regulator of inflammation, playing a role in both the inflammatory and anti-inflammatory pathways (Ma and Hottiger, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Dysregulated activation of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway is increasingly recognized to play a role in the pathogenesis of chronic inflammatory diseases, metabolic inflammatory diseases and cancer.
source: Dysregulated activation of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway is increasingly recognized to play a role in the pathogenesis of chronic inflammatory diseases, metabolic inflammatory diseases and cancer (Jridi et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Mice fed on a high-fat Western-type diet expressed high concentrations of Wnt2 protein in atherosclerotic lesions, suggesting that the Wnt/β-catenin pathway also contributes to atherosclerosis.
source: Mice fed on a high-fat Western-type diet expressed high concentrations of Wnt2 protein in atherosclerotic lesions, suggesting that the Wnt/β-catenin pathway also contributes to atherosclerosis (Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The findings reveal significant differences in inflammatory and metabolic proteins and pathways between healthy individuals living in East Africa and individuals living in Western Europe.
source: To summarize, our findings reveal significant differences in inflammatory and metabolic proteins and pathways between healthy individuals living in East Africa and individuals living in Western Europe.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the differential expression analysis.

claim: The findings are especially important in light of the current epidemiological transition and lifestyle changes in sub-Saharan Africa, which coincides with a sharp increase in non-communicable diseases in the region.
source: This is especially important in light of the current epidemiological transition and lifestyle changes in sub-Saharan Africa, which coincides with a sharp increase in non-communicable diseases in the region.
evidence: This is an inference about the importance of the findings in the context of public health trends.

claim: The study endorses the importance of including underrepresented populations in systems-immunology studies.
source: Our study also endorses the importance of including underrepresented populations in systems-immunology studies.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the broader implications of the study for research practices.

claim: The 300TZFG cohort consists of 323 healthy Tanzanian individuals aged between 18 and 65 years residing in the Kilimanjaro region in Northern Tanzania.
source: Briefly, the 300TZFG cohort consists of 323 healthy Tanzanian individuals aged between 18 and 65 years residing in the Kilimanjaro region in Northern Tanzania.
evidence: This is a description of the study cohort.

claim: The 300TZFG cohort was enrolled between March and December 2017.
